title: Kenyan Tomato Basil Soup
community: Urban Kenya — the café and restaurant soup staple
author: Mama Wanjiru
desc: Kenyan Tomato Basil Soup — vine-ripened tomatoes and garlic roasted until caramelised, blended with fresh basil, vegetable stock, and olive oil into a silky, intensely flavoured soup. Kenya's tomatoes make this soup far superior to the tinned version.
longDesc: Tomato basil soup made with freshly roasted Kenyan tomatoes has an intensity that tinned tomato soup cannot approach. Kenya produces excellent tomatoes year-round and the roasted version — caramelised and concentrated in the oven — produces a soup of extraordinary depth.
ingredients: Cream or coconut cream — to swirl, optional
steps: Place tomatoes cut-side up, onion halves, and garlic head on a baking tray. Drizzle with olive oil and salt.
Roast for 25—30 minutes until caramelised and slightly charred at the edges.
Transfer everything to a blender with stock and basil.
Strain for an ultra-smooth restaurant finish.
Warm gently. Add sugar, salt, and pepper to taste.
Serve with a cream swirl and fresh basil.
chefTips: The charred edges are not burnt — they are flavour. Do not discard them.
Fresh basil goes in at the blending stage — not during roasting.
The sugar balances the tomato acidity — taste before deciding how much.
commonMistakes: Cooking the basil — it turns black and bitter.
cookingScience: Roasting concentrates tomato flavours by evaporating 60—70% of their water while simultaneously caramelising natural sugars and creating Maillard compounds from the amino acids and sugars. This produces a soup with 3—4x the flavour intensity of raw or boiled tomato soup.
sustainabilityTips: Kenyan tomatoes are grown year-round in Kirinyaga, Kiambu, and Mwea — completely locally sourced.
healthBenefits: Roasted tomatoes have higher lycopene bioavailability than raw.
Rich in vitamins A and C.
culturalNote: Tomato basil soup made with Kenya's excellent fresh tomatoes demonstrates what can be achieved when good local ingredients are treated with proper culinary technique — it bears no resemblance to the tinned version.
